Peak flow rate (PFR) is an important diagnostic tool in pulmonary function testing (PFTs) for evaluating airflow function. When a patient stands or sits in a position that separates the basis of the head and upper limbs from the chest wall, it helps to avoid uneven pressure above and below the diaphragm as the patient inhales or exhales. When these pressures are uneven, the measured PFR is not a good reflection of the airflow that actually flows through the lungs and is more likely to underestimate airflow. As a result, the reduction in peak flow in standing posture correlates with a large reduction in lung ventilation, erroneously suggesting that the patient is more fully ventilated. Therefore, standing or sitting in a position that separates the heart from the lower limbs or above the head, and that is fully supported by the upper and lower limbs, is recommended when a patient has the goal of gaining more capacity to ventilate and improve their outcome during a spirometry test or other PFTs. In short, this position can more accurately reflect the amount of airflow that actually flows through the lungs and is likely to improve lung function during test.
